einzeiler: Can a solar storm like the 1859 Carrington Event happen again and destroy our tech?
kurzfassung: In 1859, the Carrington Event fried global telegraph networks with a massive solar storm, raising the question of whether a similar blast could cripple modern civilization. While experts like former NASA scientist Jim Green warn that society is overdue for such a disaster, power grids remain largely unprepared. Mitigating the risk relies heavily on early warning systems and the ability to shut down vulnerable infrastructure in time.
stichpunkte: The 1859 Carrington Event was triggered by solar magnetic fields snapping and launching millions of tons of solar material toward Earth.
The resulting geomagnetic storm induced massive electrical currents in long wires, overheating and destroying telegraph equipment.
Historical records from ancient China, Japan, and Babylon show that extreme solar storms recur on a scale of centuries.
Modern infrastructure—including power grids, satellites, and the internet—remains highly vulnerable to severe space weather.
A 1989 solar storm successfully knocked out the entire power grid of Quebec, Canada, during winter.
Defending against a major solar storm requires advanced warnings, heavy load distribution, and ultimately turning off critical electrical equipment.
Government exercises reveal significant gaps in preparedness, chain of command, and response speed during severe space weather events.
Experts argue that grid operators drag their feet on installing protective circuit breakers primarily due to financial costs.

kapitel.titel: Predicting and Defending Against Space Weather

clips.text: During the historical 1859 event, telegraph hardware failed violently as power sources blew up and communication stations burned down.
An intense geomagnetic storm overwhelmed the regional electrical infrastructure, causing a complete blackout across an entire Canadian province in freezing weather.

clips.hook: You could stand in Colombia and see the aurora.
clips.text: Analysis of historical newspaper reports reveals that the 1859 solar storm produced vivid red auroras visible near the equator.

clips.hook: You're only building one a month.
clips.text: Replacing massive high-voltage transformers destroyed in a widespread blackout would take an extremely long time because they are custom-built.
While government agencies scrambled to prepare for a major real-world solar storm, everyday citizens remained completely unaware and indifferent.

beschreibung:
In 1859, the sky turned blood-red, telegraph machines sparked and chattered, and some of their batteries exploded. Then humanity responded by building a civilization that runs on electricity, satellites, GPS, internet cables, credit cards, and cellphone towers.
Great work, everyone.
Ben Bradford investigates the Carrington Event — the massive solar storm that fried the technology of its time — and asks what would happen if something like it hit our much more wired world today. Was Carrington a one-off? Are modern power grids, satellites, and internet infrastructure any safer than an 1859 telegraph? And if the sun does cough another piece of itself at us, is there anything we can actually do?
Guests:
Jim Green, former chief scientist of NASA and founder of Metavisionaries
Elizabeth Butler at the NOAA Space Weather Prediction Center
